evidenceClaims.statement: A focal small-bowel caliber change with upstream dilation and downstream collapse supports a mechanical obstruction.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Distribution alone does not establish cause or bowel viability.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with suspected or established small-bowel obstruction.

evidenceClaims.statement: A closed-loop configuration, especially with reduced mural enhancement or associated fluid, warrants prompt operative assessment for threatened bowel.
evidenceClaims.limitation: The questions combine anatomy with perfusion findings. A single minor fluid finding is not a universal operation threshold.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with suspected or established small-bowel obstruction.

evidenceClaims.statement: A lactate value in the laboratory reference interval does not exclude bowel ischemia.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Serial clinical and imaging findings determine concern. No laboratory cutoff is authored.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with suspected or established small-bowel obstruction.

evidenceClaims.statement: Presumed adhesive SBO can receive an inpatient nonoperative trial when clinical assessment and CT reveal no peritonitis, strangulation or ischemia.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Exact clinical application and competing actions require named clinician review.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with suspected or established small-bowel obstruction.

evidenceClaims.statement: In an adequately performed enteral water-soluble contrast assessment for adhesive SBO, failure to reach the colon by the 24-hour film strongly suggests nonoperative failure.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Technical adequacy and clinical trajectory matter. This is not an isolated automatic operation deadline.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with suspected or established small-bowel obstruction.

evidenceClaims.statement: Contrast transit predicts the chance of nonoperative resolution and does not override new findings concerning for ischemia or peritonitis.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Exact clinical application and competing actions require named clinician review.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with suspected or established small-bowel obstruction.

evidenceClaims.statement: New peritoneal findings or clinical deterioration during SBO care warrant timely exploration even when earlier assessment supported observation.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Exact clinical application and competing actions require named clinician review.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with suspected or established small-bowel obstruction.

evidenceClaims.statement: Absence of prior abdominal surgery does not by itself require exploration in every SBO patient when CT and examination support a supervised nonoperative trial.
evidenceClaims.limitation: WSES position paper evidence is mostly retrospective. A nonadhesive cause must still be considered.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with suspected or established small-bowel obstruction.

evidenceClaims.statement: A nonoperative SBO trial includes bowel rest, decompression when indicated, intravenous volume and electrolyte replacement, and serial surgical reassessment.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Exact clinical application and competing actions require named clinician review.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with suspected or established small-bowel obstruction.

evidenceClaims.statement: Resolution of SBO in a previously unoperated abdomen does not establish its cause and should be followed by evaluation for an underlying lesion when indicated.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One adequate retrieved position paper. It does not specify a universal modality, surveillance interval or cancer-screening pathway.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with suspected or established small-bowel obstruction.

evidenceClaims.statement: Regional citrate can extend CRRT circuit life in adults at high bleeding risk when citrate use is appropriate.
evidenceClaims.limitation: The preference over no anticoagulation is conditional. Systemic anticoagulation needs and metabolic risk alter the decision.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with surgical or general critical illness and AKI. Pediatric and chronic maintenance-dialysis decisions are excluded.

evidenceClaims.statement: Citrate anticoagulation requires monitoring of systemic ionized calcium and metabolic changes.
evidenceClaims.limitation: No universal infusion recipe or monitoring interval is authored.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with surgical or general critical illness and AKI. Pediatric and chronic maintenance-dialysis decisions are excluded.

evidenceClaims.statement: A monitored trial off CRRT can be considered when spontaneous urine output and current metabolic and volume needs suggest sufficient kidney support.
evidenceClaims.limitation: There is no universal successful-weaning urine cutoff. Reassess and restart if needed.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with surgical or general critical illness and AKI. Pediatric and chronic maintenance-dialysis decisions are excluded.

evidenceClaims.statement: A low creatinine during CRRT can reflect treatment removal and does not establish independent kidney recovery.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One guideline explicitly explains production, native elimination and treatment removal. Use the observed interruption course.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with surgical or general critical illness and AKI. Pediatric and chronic maintenance-dialysis decisions are excluded.

evidenceClaims.statement: Creatinine and urine-output trajectories should be integrated with the clinical course when assessing AKI.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Creatinine lags changes in filtration and is affected by fluid distribution and treatment clearance.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with surgical or general critical illness and AKI. Pediatric and chronic maintenance-dialysis decisions are excluded.

evidenceClaims.statement: Hemodynamically stable adults with an ongoing replacement need may receive either continuous or intermittent kidney support.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Modality conversion does not establish that replacement remains necessary. Current requirements and local expertise govern.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with surgical or general critical illness and AKI. Pediatric and chronic maintenance-dialysis decisions are excluded.

evidenceClaims.statement: Respiratory pulse-pressure variation becomes unreliable with spontaneous respiratory effort or an irregular rhythm.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One directly inspected technical source. An arterial-line variation value does not rescue violated acquisition assumptions.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults undergoing acute hospital shock assessment and resuscitation

evidenceClaims.statement: Passive leg raising can assess preload responsiveness during spontaneous breathing or arrhythmia when its effect on flow is measured directly.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Use technically adequate flow measurement and the reversible response. Arterial pressure change and isolated IVC diameter are insufficient substitutes.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults undergoing acute hospital shock assessment and resuscitation

evidenceClaims.statement: Dynamic flow response is more useful than static filling pressure for predicting a cardiac-output response to further volume expansion.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Predicting a cardiac-output response does not establish clinical benefit or a mandate to give fluid.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults undergoing acute hospital shock assessment and resuscitation

evidenceClaims.statement: Respiratory vena-caval variation has important acquisition and physiologic limitations, especially during spontaneous breathing.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One directly inspected technical source. No universal caval-diameter cutoff is authored and no isolated caval observation establishes fluid responsiveness.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults undergoing acute hospital shock assessment and resuscitation

evidenceClaims.statement: A positive preload-response test requires a separate assessment of hypoperfusion and fluid-related harm before a bolus is chosen.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Risk-benefit assessment is individualized. No source establishes the numerical patient observations as a universal treatment cutoff.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults undergoing acute hospital shock assessment and resuscitation

evidenceClaims.statement: Norepinephrine is the preferred initial vasopressor for septic shock with persistent hypotension and preserved cardiac systolic function.
evidenceClaims.limitation: SSC 2026 allows either norepinephrine or epinephrine with concomitant cardiac dysfunction. These initial cases explicitly retain preserved systolic function.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults undergoing acute hospital shock assessment and resuscitation

evidenceClaims.statement: Dobutamine added to norepinephrine is an option for septic cardiac dysfunction with ongoing hypoperfusion despite adequate pressure and volume assessment.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Very-low-certainty SSC recommendation. Epinephrine is another supported strategy. This packet does not offer both as mutually exclusive keys or claim a survival benefit.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults undergoing acute hospital shock assessment and resuscitation

evidenceClaims.statement: An achieved arterial-pressure target does not establish adequate cardiac output or tissue perfusion.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Interpret serial perfusion, flow and ventricular findings together. No isolated catheter value diagnoses the shock mechanism.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults undergoing acute hospital shock assessment and resuscitation

evidenceClaims.statement: A preserved left-ventricular contraction observation from incomplete transthoracic imaging does not assess unvisualized right-sided or pericardial structures.
evidenceClaims.limitation: The inference is limited to the structures actually acquired. A missing exported image and a documented failed acoustic window are different problems.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults undergoing acute hospital shock assessment and resuscitation

evidenceClaims.statement: TEE can provide structural cardiac assessment when persistent shock remains unexplained and transthoracic windows cannot provide the needed views.
evidenceClaims.limitation: TEE requires trained acquisition and procedure-specific safety assessment. The current cohort concerns cardiovascular ICU practice. This fictional patient's postoperative window problem is an acquisition-based application, requiring clinician review.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults undergoing acute hospital shock assessment and resuscitation

evidenceClaims.statement: Ultrasound contrast can improve endocardial-border definition during echocardiographic assessment of ventricular contraction.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One directly inspected review. This supports the contrast-TTE competitor under an appropriate border-definition problem. It does not establish that contrast restores a physically inaccessible transthoracic acoustic path.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults undergoing acute hospital shock assessment and resuscitation

evidenceClaims.statement: Bedside echocardiography helps distinguish cardiac, obstructive and mixed mechanisms when shock persists despite initial treatment.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Echo findings require clinical interpretation. First-line echo is not a claim that all other testing or advanced monitoring is unnecessary.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults undergoing acute hospital shock assessment and resuscitation

evidenceClaims.statement: Infiltrative malignant glands distinguish appendiceal adenocarcinoma from a noninfiltrative low-grade mucinous neoplasm.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One directly verified current specialty guideline. A fully evaluated permanent specimen is supplied in the draft. A small biopsy or uncertain frozen section would not establish the same extent.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Permanent pathology assessment of an appendectomy specimen.

evidenceClaims.statement: Nonmetastatic appendiceal adenocarcinoma generally warrants oncologic right hemicolectomy with regional nodal assessment.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One directly verified current specialty guideline, recommendation 13. The draft has invasion into mesoappendiceal fat, adequate staging and a fit patient. The recommendation is not generalized to isolated LAMN or disseminated peritoneal disease.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Fit adults with invasive appendiceal adenocarcinoma and no distant or peritoneal metastases.

evidenceClaims.statement: Appendectomy is sufficient surgical treatment for a margin-negative LAMN with an intact wall and no peritoneal involvement.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One directly verified current specialty guideline, recommendation 12. Used for counterfactuals and the boundary against invasive carcinoma. Surveillance details remain outside the scored task.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Completely resected, nonperforated LAMN without peritoneal disease.

evidenceClaims.statement: Selected patients with appendiceal mucinous neoplasia and peritoneal dissemination merit peritoneal-surface surgical assessment for cytoreduction and intraperitoneal treatment.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One directly verified current specialty guideline, recommendations 13-15. Right colectomy does not by itself address diffuse peritoneal disease. Systemic chemotherapy has limited activity in low-grade disease. Referral does not assert that every patient is operable or requires one HIPEC regimen.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: A fit patient with biopsy-confirmed low-grade appendiceal mucinous peritoneal disease and no distant solid-organ metastases.

evidenceClaims.statement: A permanent biopsy containing low-grade mucinous epithelium in a deposit outside the appendix establishes cellular extra-appendiceal disease in that sampled site; an acellular sample from another site does not negate it.
evidenceClaims.limitation: ASCRS 2025 recommendations 2, 11 and 14 support representative biopsy, tissue-based cellularity and limitations of cytology. The conclusion is confined to represented tissue, not a claim that all deposits share that grade or that cytology should be routinely ordered.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Separately labelled mucin and solid-nodule samples obtained at appendectomy.

evidenceClaims.statement: Infiltrative appendiceal goblet-cell epithelial tumors follow an adenocarcinoma treatment pathway despite possible focal neuroendocrine-marker expression.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One directly verified current specialty guideline. The exact diagnosis is confirmed on expert permanent review. A stain result by itself is insufficient to reclassify the tumor.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Localized appendiceal goblet cell adenocarcinoma.

evidenceClaims.statement: An abnormal appendix encountered incidentally can be removed intact with a grossly clear base, preserving definitive specimen assessment before deciding on oncologic colectomy.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One directly verified current specialty guideline, recommendation 2. The base and extent govern resection. Suspected mucinous lesions require avoidance of rupture. No automatic operation is specified for extensive peritoneal disease.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: An incidentally dilated, unruptured appendix with a separable uninvolved base and no peritoneal deposits.

evidenceClaims.statement: A subcentimeter appendiceal NET without unfavorable features can be treated by appendectomy that includes the mesoappendix.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One directly verified current specialty guideline, recommendation 7. Used as a counterfactual boundary. This packet supplies no universal rule for 1-2-cm tumors or a surveillance schedule.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: A completely removed appendiceal NET smaller than 1 cm with favorable histology.

evidenceClaims.statement: A liver lesion with homogeneous fluid signal, a thin smooth wall and no enhancing internal tissue on adequate contrast MRI has the characteristic morphology of a simple hepatic cyst.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Publisher full text and CC BY 4.0 verified. This is a narrow morphology claim, not a claim that a negative receptor scan excludes all liver metastases. Imaging must actually resolve the represented lesions.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adequate precontrast, fluid-sensitive and postcontrast liver MRI of previously indeterminate lesions.

evidenceClaims.statement: For a nonmetastatic appendiceal NET larger than 2 cm, right hemicolectomy addresses the regional nodal basin even after a margin-negative appendectomy.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One directly verified current specialty guideline, recommendation 7. The exact greater-than-2-cm threshold is directly stated there. Management of tumors measuring 1-2 cm is withheld as a disputed boundary.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: A fit adult with a 2.6-cm well-differentiated appendiceal NET and no distant disease.

evidenceClaims.statement: Somatostatin-receptor PET/CT can clarify staging of a well-differentiated appendiceal NET when cross-sectional imaging leaves possible metastases unresolved.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One directly verified current specialty guideline, recommendation 5. Ga-DOTA PET/CT is favored over older receptor scintigraphy for sensitivity and over FDG PET/CT in well-differentiated NETs. Exact comparative performance estimates are excluded.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Patients with appendiceal NETs larger than 2 cm or indeterminate metastatic findings.

evidenceClaims.statement: A high-risk blunt mechanism with nonspecific bowel or mesenteric CT abnormalities warrants inpatient observation with serial assessment rather than reassurance from absence of free air.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One guideline; limited to stable, clinically evaluable patients without a direct operative sign. This is not a blanket rule after a completely normal high-quality CT.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: A traumatic bowel-wall defect or convincing extraluminal enteric contrast is a direct indication for prompt surgical exploration.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One guideline; isolated free fluid or mesenteric stranding does not carry the same implication.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: In a sustained stable or stabilized adult without an immediate operative indication, IV-contrast CT characterizes abdominal injury beyond what FAST can exclude.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Negative FAST is not a general exclusion of visceral or retroperitoneal injury; no sensitivity number is taught.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: Evolving suspicion after an equivocal initial bowel CT can justify repeat CT while the patient remains stable and has not developed an operative indication.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One guideline; repeat imaging must not delay operation for peritonitis or instability. The question does not teach a fixed interval.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: After an equivocal initial CT in suspected blunt bowel injury, WSES supports CT reassessment after a six-hour interval; an evolving suspicious course also supports repeat imaging.
evidenceClaims.limitation: This is a guideline reassessment recommendation for selected equivocal or evolving presentations, not a mandatory universal scan clock, a gameplay wait estimate, or a reason to delay operation for peritonitis. One guideline publication directly supports the six-hour value.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with traumatic abdominal injury receiving hospital care, reviewed here as outside-hospital clinic records.

evidenceClaims.statement: Persistent circulatory deterioration after resuscitation together with intraperitoneal fluid on FAST supports urgent trauma laparotomy rather than transport for CT.
evidenceClaims.limitation: A transient pressure rise does not establish sustained stabilization; this claim does not choose among hybrid-suite interventions in a sustained responder.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: Persistent pelvic hemorrhage after angiography despite pelvic stabilization is an indication to consider preperitoneal packing for bleeding not controlled by an arterial procedure.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One older guideline publication; does not rank initial packing against immediate angiography in every center or select orthopedic fixation.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: Persistent pelvic bleeding with an arterial CT focus after stabilization or packing supports angiography and possible selective embolization, including repeat angiography.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One older guideline; arterial and nonarterial bleeding may coexist. An isolated fracture pattern does not identify the bleeding source.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: Absence of intraperitoneal fluid on FAST does not exclude pelvic retroperitoneal hemorrhage.
evidenceClaims.limitation: It also does not prove the pelvis is the only source; associated thoracic, abdominal and external sources must be assessed.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: Multiphase trauma CT can distinguish an enlarging pool of extravasated arterial contrast from a contained vascular sac that follows blood-pool enhancement.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One guideline supports active-versus-contained vascular interpretation. The constructed report is text, not a simulated scan or a performance claim.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the specific abdominal/pelvic injury and care phase described in the mapped draft.

evidenceClaims.statement: Gross hematuria after blunt pelvic trauma warrants retrograde cystography, using conventional radiography or a CT cystogram.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Cystography follows urgent hemorrhage control. If urethral injury is suspected, urethral assessment precedes catheter placement.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: Renally excreted contrast reaching a partially filled bladder on ordinary trauma CT does not substitute for retrograde bladder distension during cystography.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One guideline publication; distinguishes an unperformed adequate acquisition from a missing exported image series.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: Delayed excretory imaging evaluates urinary extravasation and ureteral continuity beyond the arterial and venous trauma CT phases.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One guideline publication; does not require an invented acquisition delay or presume a missing series was never acquired.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: When traumatic urethral injury is suspected, retrograde urethrography or appropriate urethroscopy evaluates the urethra; urethral assessment precedes bladder catheterization when feasible.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Single guideline; modality varies with sex and specific injury. The mapped patient already has documented atraumatic catheter access.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the specific abdominal/pelvic injury and care phase described in the mapped draft.

evidenceClaims.statement: Bladder-neck involvement, intravesical bone injury or associated rectal/vaginal injury can make an extraperitoneal bladder rupture a repair problem rather than simple catheter care.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Do not equate a pelvic fracture by itself with every listed complex feature; the precise boundary remains for clinician review.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: Uncomplicated traumatic extraperitoneal bladder rupture can be treated with catheter drainage rather than routine repair.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Complex injuries, adjacent organ injury and planned relevant pelvic surgery may alter management. WSES wording around fracture-associated complexity is broader than EAST; no fracture-alone repair rule is taught.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: A distal pancreatic transection with main-duct disruption is a resectional injury; distal pancreatectomy is supported in a stable adult requiring operative treatment.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Both guidelines are conditional/low-quality here. Proximal injuries and endoscopically bridgeable selected injuries need a different discussion; the draft is an intraoperative distal complete transection.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: A minor pancreatic injury with an intact main duct generally permits nonresectional management; intraoperative drainage may be used.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Duct status must be adequately assessed, not inferred from a normal early enzyme value.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: If duct integrity remains uncertain after CT, further duct assessment with MRCP or ERCP can change pancreatic injury management.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Neither option is ranked universally; the draft does not claim a normal MRCP invariably excludes duct injury or rank the two tests.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: Destructive duodenopancreatic injury may need complex reconstruction; shock favors damage control with reconstruction staged by experienced teams.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One guideline; do not teach routine pancreaticoduodenectomy or pyloric exclusion for an otherwise repairable duodenal tear.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: Pancreaticojejunostomy is a described specialist reconstructive option in selected severe pancreatic injuries; limited evidence does not make it routine for isolated distal duct transection.
evidenceClaims.limitation: WSES describes selected reconstructions; EAST includes very limited severe-injury reports. This is an existence/selection boundary, not a rule favoring Roux-en-Y reconstruction for every proximal injury.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the specific abdominal/pelvic injury and care phase described in the mapped draft.

evidenceClaims.statement: During exploration of an unstable adult trauma patient, a stable nonexpanding zone-II renal hematoma need not be opened; instability may come from another injury.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Conditional EAST 2023 recommendation from limited observational data. Stable describes the hematoma, not the patient. Do not generalize to an expanding/pulsatile hematoma or central vascular injury.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: When an expanding renal hematoma requires intervention, kidney-preserving techniques are conditionally favored over automatic nephrectomy when feasible.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Conditional low-quality evidence; life-saving nephrectomy remains possible when repair cannot control hemorrhage.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: A viable nondestructive small-bowel laceration can undergo primary repair; loss of more than half the circumference or mesenteric devascularization argues against that repair.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One guideline; the greater-than-50% boundary is directly stated in its primary-repair section. No universal suture technique or mandatory stoma rule is taught.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: After necessary small-bowel resection, viable bowel and restored physiology can support immediate anastomosis; unresolved perfusion, resuscitation or control tasks can favor staged reconstruction.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Choice remains patient- and operation-specific. No exact blood, pressor, pH or contamination threshold is asserted. WSES is the direct publication; this is not independent cohort replication.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with traumatic abdominal injury receiving hospital care, reviewed here as outside-hospital clinic records.

evidenceClaims.statement: Continuing hypotension, worsening acidosis, hypothermia and coagulopathic bleeding favor an abbreviated operation with hemorrhage/contamination control and temporary abdominal closure.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Physiology and unfinished surgical tasks govern the decision; no universal numerical trigger or exact resuscitation prescription is taught.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: An open abdomen may remain necessary while resuscitation, contamination control, deferred reconstruction or reassessment of questionable bowel viability is unfinished.
evidenceClaims.limitation: One adequate guideline publication; does not imply that edema or a trauma diagnosis mandates an open abdomen.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults with abdominal or pelvic trauma in a trauma-capable hospital.

evidenceClaims.statement: In severe obstructive airflow limitation, incomplete exhalation can cause intrinsic PEEP; reducing respiratory rate can lengthen expiration and lessen trapping despite persistent hypercapnia.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Review directly supports the rate action; assessment guideline independently supports checking auto-PEEP. No numeric rate, safe pH or external-PEEP prescription is generalized.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the stated outside-hospital record; clinic encounter is retrospective review.

evidenceClaims.statement: During passive ventilation, an end-inspiratory hold measures plateau pressure and helps separate a flow-dependent peak-pressure increase from persistent static pressure loading.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Acquisition requires minimal patient effort and no major leak; unchanged delivered volume, flow and measured total PEEP are necessary for matched inference.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the stated outside-hospital record; clinic encounter is retrospective review.

evidenceClaims.statement: NIV should generally not delay reintubation for established post-extubation respiratory failure in the general non-COPD, non-postoperative population.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Conditional low-certainty guidance; COPD and postoperative populations are exceptions to generalization. Case uses medical pneumonia and worsening fatigue.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the stated outside-hospital record; clinic encounter is retrospective review.

evidenceClaims.statement: Immediate clinical deterioration during an NIV trial requires prompt reassessment for invasive ventilation rather than extending the mask trial to normalize saturation.
evidenceClaims.limitation: Single joint guideline; key case has worsening consciousness, effort and acidemia together, not a universal pH-alone intubation threshold.
evidenceClaims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the stated outside-hospital record; clinic encounter is retrospective review.
